newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. warns Manila, Beijing in islands dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Manila, Beijing in islands dispute.

text.p: The Philippines on Thursday raised the heat in its dispute with China over obscure islands in the South China Sea, and the United States warned both sides against using force to settle the issue.

Brushing aside protests from China, Philippine police filed charges of illegal entry against 21 Chinese fishermen arrested nine days ago after a dramatic boat chase off a rocky outcrop called Scarborough Shoal claimed by both Manila and Beijing. Manila filed the charges after diplomats of the two countries ended three days of talks in Beijing on Wednesday without resolving their disputes over the islands. But they agreed "to exercise self-restraint", the Philippine foreign ministry said.
But a Philippine Navy official threw doubt on the charges, saying the fishermen may have been innocent despite the chase in which the Navy twice shot across their ship's bow.
He said in a report that they were carrying fish which did not seem to come from Scarborough Shoal waters.
The downswing in relations between the two Asian neighbours has spurred Philippine officials to call for a strengthening of Manila's defence pact with Washington.
They are acutely aware the Philippines, left alone to defend itself after it closed the last of two huge U.S. military bases on its soil five years ago, is no match for Chinese armed forces.

U.S. Ambassador Thomas Hubbard rejected any revision of a defence treaty, which can help Manila in case of attack only with U.S. Congressional approval, and warned claimants to South China Sea islands against using force to settle their quarrels.

"We would strongly oppose any effort to solve this problem by using force and we have made known to all parties of the region that we encourage their efforts to solve the problem," Hubbard told reporters after meeting President Fidel Ramos.

He said the treaty was "a good document that serves our mutual interest...We're happy where it now stands". The 1951 treaty calls on both countries to come to each other's aid if one is attacked but some Filipino officials would like to see the need for Congressional approval removed.
Philippine Senate minority leader Francisco Tatad called for "an automatic retaliation clause...to repel aggression instantly in case the Philippines is attacked" in the South China Sea.
The row with China has exposed the helplessness of the Philippines' military, with an air force composed of 10 Vietnam War-vintage fighter jets and a navy of 40-year-old ships.

Armed forces chief General Arnulfo Acedera underlined the country's vulnerability when he sounded out U.S. officials in recent talks on possible American help if the Philippines were threatened by "a superior force".

The dispute has also spurred Manila to speed up its $2 billion programme to upgrade military hardware. It has set Friday as the deadline for foreign suppliers to submit their bids for fighter jets for the Philippine Air Force. The Chinese foreign ministry on Thursday again called on the Philippines to release the fishermen, saying Manila had "seriously infringed on Chinese sovereignty".

Besides the dispute over Scarborough Shoal, the two countries are also contesting the Spratly Islands, a potentially oil-rich cluster of islets, reefs and atolls also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei. Beijing says the sea historically belongs to China. Despite the growing public hostility, at their talks in Bejing senior diplomats from the two countries "agree d...to calm the atmosphere...(and) to avoid acts that tend to destabilise the situation", a Philippine foreign ministry statement said. It said they agreed to convene a working group "to work out measures to ensure these disputes do not develop into conflict".
